references.text: Describes how the famine affected the entire region and how people from other countries came to Egypt to buy grain – the background for why Egyptians eventually had to sell their land.
Provides context on how Egyptians gradually used up their money, sold their livestock, and finally offered their land and themselves to Pharaoh in exchange for food during the famine.
Describes the follow-up to Joseph buying all the land: he gives the people seed and establishes the law that one-fifth of the harvest belongs to Pharaoh.
Refers to how Joseph was made ruler over Pharaoh's house and to rule over all his property, a position of power that enabled the purchase of Egypt's land.
Joseph prophesies about the seven years of famine that would come after the seven good years – the direct cause for why Egyptians eventually had to sell their land.
Highlights the progressive famine that forced Egyptians to sell their properties.
Explains the economic process (money) that led to the land becoming Pharaoh's property.
Emphasizes the global famine that made Joseph's intervention necessary for the entire region.
Marks the transition where Pharaoh gives Joseph full authority to handle the crisis and later buy the country.
Creates a theological contrast by showing that Joseph's family retained their property while others lost everything.
Explains the lasting legal consequence of the land becoming Pharaoh's property.
The report on the start of the famine that created the conditions for the sale of the land.
Confirms Joseph's authority and actions as directly leading to the people having to sell their land.
